10.1002_adfm.78308: The development of new electrolytes for metal‐ion batteries is currently constrained by the inefficiency of trial‐and‐error exploration across vast chemical spaces. Here, we establish a comprehensive framework for chemical descriptor‐based inverse electrolyte design that maps target electrolyte properties back to molecular, polymeric, and lattice‐level building blocks. By extracting fundamental chemical descriptors, we decompose electrolyte performance into electrochemical stability, ionic transport, electronic leakage, thermal safety, and lifecycle constraints, challenging classical frontier‐orbital (highest occupied molecular orbital/lowest unoccupied molecular orbital) criteria for electrochemical stability by accounting for the electron/hole addition perturbations and the critical role of interfacial effects. Addressing ion transport, we unify optimization strategies across phases, linking solvation structures in liquids and lattice defects in solids to minimize impedance via atomic‐level ion transport control. We decouple the origins of electronic leakage, distinguishing between structural‐defect‐induced pathways and parasitic redox transport. On safety, we trace thermal runaway to molecular thermodynamics. Integrating lifecycle constraints, we analyse how manufacturing defects and abuse conditions compromise these theoretical designs. Furthermore, to address the data‐scarcity bottleneck in data‐driven discovery, we propose the “Minimum Information for Electrolyte Studies and Cells” (MIESC) checklist and advocate systematic reporting of negative results to establish robust decision boundaries. This work thus provides a roadmap for rationally designing next‐generation electrolytes.
10.1002_anie.5562966: Ultrafine metal oxide nanoclusters (UMONs) exhibit remarkable catalytic potential due to their high specific surface area; however, achieving precise control over both the size and crystal phase of UMONs remains a significant challenge. Herein, we developed a dual‐induced confined synthesis strategy that couples hydrophobic gating with thermally triggered phase transformation to precisely confine UMONs within the pores of a metal–organic framework (MOF). 13 UMONs@MOF composites were successfully synthesized with the metal cations in UMONs spanning different regions of the periodic table. Notably, sub‐3 nm metastable γ‐MnO 2 was stabilized and confined within MIL‐101(Fe) for the first time. The optimized 15% γ‐MnO 2 @MIL‐101(Fe) showed a durable 100% O 3 removal efficiency for over 100 h. This performance was maintained in a continuous air flow containing 40 ppm O 3 at a high gas hourly space velocity of 1.7 × 10 5 h −1 over a wide humidity range of 10%–90%. Mechanistic studies reveal that its superior catalytic activity originates from the synergistic effect between the confined γ‐MnO 2 active sites and the Fe 3 O clusters in the MIL‐101(Fe). This work provides a universal approach for the precise control of the size and crystal phase of UMONs, paving the way for designing high‐performance catalysts.
10.1002_anie.6468533: Electrochemical H 2 O 2 synthesis through the two‐electron oxygen reduction reaction offers a sustainable alternative to the energy‐intensive anthraquinone process. Crystalline porous frameworks are attractive for this route because of their structural precision, yet poor electrolyte wetting and limited electrochemical accessibility often restrict their practical performance. Here, we report an interfacial charge‐modulation strategy that transforms covalent metal–organic frameworks into highly wetted and electrochemically accessible catalytic interfaces. By incorporating cationic ethidium bromide units into a trinuclear copper‐pyrazolate framework, we construct EB‐Cu 3 ‐COF featuring enlarged interlayer spacing, enhanced interfacial charge transfer, and optimized *OOH intermediate adsorption. Consequently, EB‐Cu 3 ‐COF achieves up to 99% H 2 O 2 selectivity and a flow‐cell production rate of 39 420 mmol·g cat −1 ·h −1 , ranking among the best‐performing non‐pyrolyzed porous organic electrocatalysts reported to date. This work establishes interfacial charge‐modulation as a design principle for translating crystalline structural precision into electrochemically active interfaces.
10.1002_smll.202511207: Atomic single metal sites riveted on carbon materials have drawn ever‐growing interest in various electrocatalytic and inorganic transformation processes owing to their exceptional catalytic performance and selectivity. However, there are challenges for the generic and controlled fabrication of such catalysts. Herein, a general, flexible and versatile cascade‐locking route is developed to construct metal single atom sites on hierarchical nitrogen‐doped superstructured carbons (M SAs‐N/SC) via pyrolysis of a unique metallo‐supramolecular organic framework precursor, in which primary metal complexes of 2, 2′‐bicinchoninic acid (BCA) and target metal ions using metal‐N coordination bonds are ulteriorly crosslinked with melamine (MA) units through intramolecular N─H∙∙∙O and O─H∙∙∙N hydrogen bond interactions. Importantly, a series of atomic‐level metal site catalysts can be successfully fabricated, demonstrating the remarkable adjustability and generality of this method. When acting as a heterogeneous catalyst in C‐H oxidation and alkene epoxidation reactions, such Fe SAs‐N/SC exhibited high selectivity, reusability, and substrate tolerance. Moreover, the as‐prepared Fe SAs‐N/SC catalyst delivered exceptional catalytic performance for the electrocatalytic CO 2 reduction reaction. The finding puts forward a brand‐new and universal way to synthesize single atom metal site catalysts for a wide range of potential applications.
